title: Why you still need a Website Portfolio, even though everyone can Vibe Code it.
author: FrancisTRᴅᴇᴠ
body:
If you have been following me for a long time, you already know that I have been holding off on my Portfolio review for several months. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/55r34irqjs415ihk0o1e.gif)   **Before you ask, yes, I will finally show my portfolio website.** First, I want to write about something we all may have been thinking about at some point.   **Everyone needs a developer portfolio.** It's one of the big ways to stand out in the tech market because it shows your work and experience to recruiters in a friendly UI format. Some may say it's a great alternative to review a candidate's work **(Source: Trust me bro).** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7h8pveibft5pc28guc01.png) However, in the age of AI, it seems that it's almost impossible to create a portfolio that stands out. **Why is that the case?**   ## AI Can do...anything? We all (probably) have tried using AI at some point and even still use AI in our daily lives. Whether how much you have used it, you probably already know its capabilities. **AI is trained so well that it can potentially one-shot a website portfolio.** Even better, if the person decides, it can add features and other stuff to make the website look like it was built in months (even though it was built in minutes). We even got to the point where **Claude was able to merge two games into one in a matter of a few weeks!** {% embed https://www.youtube.com/shorts/xo3vpvbA8p8 %} **It's crazy isn't it.** AI development has been rapidly growing in the last few years to the point where it is accomplishing tasks that may have taken months to do. With that said, I thought to myself: **"Why consider building a portfolio if everyone can vibe code their way into making their perfect portfolio?"** To be honest, it's a valid question. The market has been difficult because **everyone is using AI to their advantage to stand out from the market.** I have seen a lot of Website Portfolios and Resumes that have been assisted with AI. **As a result, the bar has never been higher.** However, I still believe having a portfolio still matters, even in this age where it seems impossible. **Here's my reasoning.**   ---   ## AI Portfolios may look different, but they are the same. **What do I mean by this?** I am talking about **"style".** If you try to vibe code a portfolio, people can tell that the portfolio is vibe coded. Sure, it's not the EXACT replica compare to 100 portfolios out there, but you can easily tell by seeing some UI features that are defaulted if you vaguely prompt it. A small example is this: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/1floz2r2trb7qglvp6l7.png) I have reviewed a lot of portfolios that has this (or something similar). Sure this may be a coincidence, but I want you to try to vibe code a sample website portfolio. Most of the time, they will add this feature. This matters because if you think about it, a lot of portfolios out there are simply the same, **even though it may not look like it.** You have to have good "attention to detail" to see this for sure. However, at this point, coming from a person who has reviewed candidates before, it tends to be **really repetitive.** Hence, making it harder in the hiring process since everyone is doing the same thing and more research needs to be accounted for. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/otitvym1xxhlr917bsuf.png) This leads to the next point.   ## "New Mask, Same Task" ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/iyhst5tknfvs08r0i8wn.png) **Yes, I took this straight up from RDJ.** Though the whole point is that even though he plays a different character, **he is still RDJ.** **What does this mean in this context?** Just because you have pretty portfolio, **it does not mean your work reflects that.** You can create many different portfolios under your name. At the end of the day, **it's still you that needs to improve and not the portfolio.** **Portfolio is used as a presentation.** If you are presenting your portfolio and it looks good, I would assume you have a lot of work experience and projects that are noticeable based on your portfolio design and how you are selling yourself. For example, you have a front-end developer portfolio, **but if I were to investigate further into your GitHub, I may see the following things:** - You just joined as of this year on GitHub. - You claimed you did Open-Source, but there is no PR that reflects that. - Your Portfolio has good UI, your project doesn't. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hqqedl0o60hmgy3vmbwq.png) I can list a lot of things, but the main point is that if you have a good portfolio with a good list of projects you have done, **you better hope that your projects and work reflects on how you built this portfolio.** This is **ESPECIALLY** true if you tried to become a front-end developer. If your UI is good, you better hope your projects reflects that. It's something to keep in mind when building your portfolio. Of course, if you are applying for a back-end developer role, having a good UI on your website portfolio isn't really required, but it's a nice to have. **The whole point is to not misrepresent yourself. Be careful on what you add on your portfolio. Always assume people will have questions on your work.**     Those are the two main things. Though you may be asking **"How do I make my portfolio stand out"?** **Here are some key things that you can do (and yes, I am now showing my portfolio lol).**   ---   ## 1. Start with a basic portfolio template, then use AI to add onto it. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/nl747eyej271ayfn2iit.png) For my case, I have used an existing portfolio from **"brittanychiang.com and meikopoulos.com"**. From there, I grab existing features using AI and put them together into a portfolio I am proud of. Additionally, I added some new features that are not distracting, but is something I want to add onto my portfolio to make it unique to me: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/y6mihaafktq4gfkff5ut.png) **Instead of building it from scratch, I encourage you to find a portfolio that already exists (Bonus points: Proven that it stands out in the tech market) and build it on top of it.** This allows the portfolio to be unique and that **reflects you.** Additionally, building on to of a template is a good starting point because it already has the fundamentals on what makes a portfolio "good". In this case, I added a feature where the "Skills" section reveals Pokemon in each Skill Card, though I am not sharing how it works. **Can you find the Easter egg that does that?** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vvvd3q57f49bbfmctdxz.png)   ## 2. Usability and Accessibility! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/kqbmxzxpo3fhlxop36kf.png) **This is the most OVERLOOK aspect of making a portfolio.** Even though you can make your portfolio look nice, it's most likely that it's **not accessible.** **For example, it can be very laggy on low-end devices, not responsive on mobile, not following best practices, etc.** There are a lot of things that is overlooked because we focus on building the best looking portfolio where we should be focusing on making our website portfolio optimized. I would recommend spending time using AI to optimize your portfolio. In other words: **"Boil the lake to make the portfolio, but boil the ocean for website optimization and accessibility".** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/shabozho5fs63ftadpah.png) **For mine, I spend countless prompts where I tell the AI to make sure my portfolio is less "laggy" and being able to run on mobile.** This will allow to make a much cleaner portfolio and being able to be used by many people such as people who have disabilities, devices that are not powerful, etc.   ## 3. Simplicity beats Complexity! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3jdxudp8a03vvlni8jvj.png) **A lot of portfolios we have seen tends to be very complex where there are a lot of animations and such.** However, the more you think about it, the more you realized that you can **stand out easily.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8pa5pdohs07xc78ycnsv.png) I have seen a lot of portfolios that are REALLY complex and have a lot of animations, but what people fail to realized is that: **You are doing what everyone else is doing.** **At the end of the day, you are not standing out, even if you THINK that you are.** If I see a portfolio that is heavily designed using AI, I can guarantee that I can find the exact same person who can one-up that. **The best advice is making it simple.** Yes, it's boring and yes it's common. But..that's the whole point. I rarely see any portfolio that is simply built. **Usually the ones that are simple tends to stand out because it shows a lot of information really quickly.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/yprh442j56lfeei9e71u.png) **This is huge because recruiters tends to review portfolios and resumes in seconds.** They will not have time to look over your awesome UI and animation you have Vibe Coded. The UI should be the icing on the cake, not the whole cake. **The most important parts is your work and experience.** Then why design your portfolio? It makes it much easier for people to navigate your work and experience than reading your resume line-by-line of course lol. The point is not spending time making the UI look nice, but **spending more time on making sure they are able to access your work and experience within a small amount of clicks.**   ## 4. Networking (AKA show your portfolio) This is the biggest thing. **SHOW YOUR PORTFOLIO.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/k81pc52mdsl6gld3udrp.gif)
Don't know what your talking about lol
  **What's the point of making a portfolio if no one is going to see it.** You can share it to your family, friends, your LinkedIn connections, and even on DEV! **With that said, here is my portfolio. Give it a review and let me know what you think!** {% embed https://francistrdev.github.io/ %}   ---   **Speaking of, if you have a portfolio that has been sitting around, feel free to share your portfolio in the comments. I would love to see your portfolio and review them!** **That is all! Cya :D**

comments.text:
A portfolio doesn’t necessarily mean you have to show your previous jobs or internship experience.

It’s basically a place where you show "what you can build and what you’re capable of".

So in your case, you can include:

"Your OSS projects

"Personal projects you’ve built

"Interesting experiments or animations you’ve made

"Projects you built while learning

"Contributions you’ve made to other open-source projects

"Case studies explaining how you solved a particular problem

You don’t have to mention your internship if you’re not comfortable sharing it publicly. Your OSS work can actually be a strong part of your portfolio because it shows real work and gives people something they can look at or interact with.

And being a student is not really a disadvantage here. If the work is good, people will care more about "what you can actually do" than whether you already have years of professional experience.

I believe with this point of mine you will be able to understand right ?

comments.author: Oleksandr
comments.text: You hit on a massive nuance here. When people say 'code execution is cheap,' they usually conflate open-source local models with corporate API billing. At enterprise scale, token counting becomes a core infrastructure cost very quickly. If your pipeline requires heavy context windows or multi-turn reasoning loops just to validate a basic Vibe Code component, that metered execution cost completely shifts the ROI. Prepaid, per-token architecture models like JZS Token make a lot of sense for capping that unpredictable bleeding. Definitely a crucial perspective to include in the economic argument.

comments.author: Jon Randy 🎖️
comments.text:
You don't need a portfolio. That simply isn't true - a total myth. They're generally just curated vanity projects that tell a potential employer next to nothing about the reality of a candidate's abilities. Far better is an active/interesting GitHub/GitLab/whatever - warts and all - false starts, finished projects, unfinished projects, contributions to other projects, unvarnished experiments... the more the better. Anyone hiring devs who knows what they're doing will glean far more from that than they would from any portfolio site.

Over thirty years as a developer I've never had a portfolio site and it's never been an issue. I also don't attach much weight to candidate portfolio sites unless they're truly awful, or exceptional/original (which is rare) - there is very little point to a cookie cutter HTML-ified CV.

In a few cases when a candidate has had a portfolio site, it has actually been the reason that they did not progress further in the hiring process... over-engineering, errors, inappropriate use of technology etc.

comments.author: FrancisTRᴅᴇᴠ
comments.text:
Hey Jon. Thanks for sharing!

I do have seen people having without portfolios and still got into jobs in this brutal market. Some of my friends who graduated didn't have a portfolio but still got a job through networking, so I see where you are coming from.

I say "need" in this case because I feel like it's a good start of having at least something to show as a good starting point in your developer journey. Of course, your first project doesn't need to be a portfolio, but it's a good starting point and it's a friendly way to showcase your future projects (if you decide to put them there). I can see where if you already have experience, then having a portfolio is just a nice thing to have, not something you need.

I believe if you are freelancing, then having a portfolio is a great thing to have because it tells you that the client not only see that this developer has experience, but also the style of the website and credibility of their work to clients. It's suitable for Front-end web developers for sure, though having it as a freelance developer in general is a must. Though, I never did freelancing before so take this as a grain of salt, but that is based on what I have seen and heard.

I am not expecting everyone to have a portfolio, but based on my experience as a beginner/mid level (in my opinion of me being a beginner/mid level) I think having a portfolio is a must and a good starting point to show your work to all audience, more than just recruiters. You may never know if the person that you share your portfolio with is impress and sharing it to their other networks.

I do have a question. When you mention "when a candidate has had a portfolio site, it has actually been the reason that they did not progress further in the hiring process... over-engineering, errors, inappropriate use of technology etc.", do recruiters or general people tend to figure out during the hiring process? How do they determine if they are using the wrong technology? I guess this is more of an elaboration?

Thanks for sharing on your view Jon! Let me know if anything!

comments.author: Anh Nguyễn Văn
comments.text: The shift toward vibe coding definitely changes how we present our work, but a portfolio serves a different purpose than just showing a functional UI. When you rely heavily on AI to scaffold projects, the "vibe" can often feel generic or lack a cohesive architectural soul. I've found that recruiters and senior leads aren't just looking at the final product anymore; they want to see the decision-making process behind the code. A portfolio that documents why you chose a specific state management pattern or how you handled a particular edge case is much more valuable than a perfectly polished, AI-generated landing page. It proves you actually understand the underlying mechanics rather than just being a prompt engineer.

I think the GitHub point is especially important here.

A portfolio can show the final result, but the repository can reveal the parts a polished UI cannot: how the project is structured, how decisions were made, how edge cases are handled, and whether the developer actually understands what they built.

The UI gets someone interested. The implementation gives them something to investigate.

Vibe coding giúp dựng UI nhanh, nhưng portfolio không chỉ là "có trang web" — nó là bằng chứng tư duy.

Khi review CV, mình quan tâm: bạn giải quyết vấn đề như thế nào? Trade-off gì giữa performance vs maintainability? Tại sao chọn stack này chứ không phải stack kia? Những quyết định này không hiện ra từ một prompt "make it pretty".

The observation that vibe-coded portfolios look different on the surface and still feel the same underneath matches what hiring managers keep saying quietly. Layout variety went up. Evidence of judgment did not.

What still separates a useful portfolio is not how fast the homepage appeared. It is whether the visitor can see a decision that cost something: a trade-off you made, a constraint you accepted, a feature you refused, or a production incident you owned. AI can invent screens. One practical habit that helps: for each project, write three lines that a model would not invent for you. Who the user was, what almost failed in production, and what you would not do the same way. That is usually enough for a recruiter to tell whether the site is a render or a record of work.

title: I left 28 unsolicited cartoons in strangers' comment threads over four days. 16 replies, 2 corrections, 0 sales. The ledger.
author: ssapable
body:
Four days ago I wrote about turning eight launch posts on DEV into short hand-drawn cartoons and leaving them in the comments, unasked. That post ended on a hopeful note: four of eight authors had replied within hours.

I kept going. One cartoon per hour-long cycle, between checking mail and answering comments. This is what the next twenty looked like, and what the whole run did and did not do.

## The rule, unchanged

Find a launch post I actually like. Turn the first screen of its README into a 45 to 100 second cartoon. Every number in the cartoon comes from the author's post. Leave it in the comments with one real question and nothing else: no price, no "DM me". If the author says a shot is wrong, re-render that shot.

## The ones since the first post

Reactions are the post's count at the moment I picked it, not later.

| Post | Cartoon | Reactions when picked |
|---|---:|---:|
| Dadi ki Rasoi, a grandmother's recipes | 57 s | 22 |
| The Almirah, a family wardrobe | 60 s | 14 |
| A dad's electricity bill dashboard | 51 s | 13 |
| Gift Hunter | 46 s | 28 |
| Campus Copilot | 54 s | 20 |
| A roguelike that lives in a GitHub profile README | 58 s | 18 |
| AphasiaBridge, built for a friend after a stroke | 70 s | 45 |
| Nivara, a WhatsApp voice-order helper for a supplement shop | 59 s | 10 |
| grill, a mock interviewer that reads a friend's Rust code | 73 s | 42 |
| Maa ka Drawer, receipt search for a mother | 75 s | 10 |
| DueDate, an eviction notice reader where code makes the decision | 75 s | 11 |
| AI Nature Quest, an outdoor game that tells you to put the phone down | 80 s | 16 |
| Drift, a walking companion that only works with the phone in your pocket | 84 s | 16 |
| BioDex, an offline plant guide running the BioCLIP encoder on the phone | 90 s | 6 |
| GoSeek, an outdoor treasure hunt that gives riddles instead of directions | 77 s | 6 |
| Equipment Field Medic, voice-guided repair with oily hands | 65 s | 7 |
| GiffyPy, a GIF editor for READMEs | 69 s | 10 |
| Screen Memory, search over what was on your screen | 67 s | 8 |
| Commit Metro, a contribution graph as a subway line | 98 s | 7 |
| BlindWalk, a screenless navigator that routes by shade and speaks by sound | 82 s | 9 |

Plus one about a home energy monitor that I rendered but never left as a comment. That makes 29 cartoons on the page and 28 comment threads. All of them, no sign-up: https://ssap-pa.github.io/scripttoon-samples/

Two things changed along the way. The cartoons got longer, from 30 to 65 seconds in the first batch to 65 to 98 seconds now, because I stopped cutting the author's second idea. And the posts I picked got smaller: the first eight averaged 25 reactions, the last ten averaged under 10. I ran out of popular posts I liked and started picking posts the day they went up, which is also where the replies got more interesting.

## What came back

Sixteen author replies across 28 threads. In their words, from the public comments:

- "Okay, I genuinely did not expect anyone to turn this into a hand-drawn video"
- "this is actually crazy"
- "What you have created is just exceptional. I just saw the video."
- "How did you do that???"
- "Its interesting thanks for sharing!"

Two corrections, both from authors who watched closely:

1. Krisp's author pointed out that the latent drift in GrooVAE moves in both directions, not one. I had drawn it as a one-way slide. Re-rendered the hook shot.
2. GiffyPy's author told me the name is pronounced "giffy-pie". The narration said "giffy-pee". Re-rendered the narration (which meant deleting one cached MP3, otherwise the pipeline reuses it).

At least six authors answered the question at the end of the comment before anything else. The questions were specific to their code: does the forecast switch from the Trends fallback to real sales automatically, does the notebook memory line go into the next prompt verbatim or summarized, how many seconds does a 1.26 GB encoder take per photo on a phone (4 to 5 on an S24 Ultra, 7 to 8 on other devices, the author said). That is the only part of this I'd call a technique: the question has to be one you can only ask after reading the code.

One author posted the cartoon on X himself and asked to connect there. One followed me. Nobody asked me to take a cartoon down.

## What it did not do

- Sales from this channel: zero. The engine behind the cartoons is a package I sell, and the samples page links to it. In four days nobody who got a cartoon, or who saw one, bought it. The one paid thing I sold in this period was a $5 copy of an unrelated book, to someone who had never seen a cartoon.
- Views: the sample videos on YouTube sat at 0 to 3 views each when I checked on day two. The X posts announcing them had a median of 6 impressions. Essentially every view came from the author and whoever read their comment thread.
- Time: about an hour per cartoon, one per cycle over four days, plus the replies. The pipeline does the drawing. Reading the post properly and writing a question that isn't generic is the part that doesn't compress.

## What I'd keep

The reply rate. Sixteen replies on 28 unsolicited comments is more conversation than anything else I have tried on this account, including a service post that offered the same thing for free and got zero replies in a day. The gifts work as conversation. They have not worked as distribution, and they have not worked as sales.

So the honest version of the lesson from four days ago is narrower than I wrote it: a finished thing plus one real question gets a reply from the person you made it for. It does not, on its own, get you anyone else.

I'll keep making them, one a cycle, because the conversations are good and the corrections make the cartoons better. If you want one for your project, the page explains how I pick. If you'd rather render your own, the engine is here: https://payhip.com/b/A2wa8

title: A Builder in New Orleans: When Your Vibecoded App Comes on Vacation
author: Earl Grey
body:
First day on Bourbon Street, and my sister and I had the most important question of the trip: where are we going to eat?
 
It should have been easy. Between the two of us, we had added sixty-eight restaurants, bars, cafés, and attractions to [Le Voyage](https://github.com/earlgreyhot1701D/le-voyage), a travel-planning app I vibecoded the better part of a year earlier. We were standing in the middle of the French Quarter, surrounded by food, carrying a small database of places we already wanted to try, and we were still hungry and indecisive.
 
So we opened the app.
 
Le Voyage started as something I built for a trip to Paris. The idea was simple. Instead of sending restaurant links back and forth, saving places in three different apps, losing recommendations in group chats, and trying to remember why somebody added a particular café three weeks ago, we could keep the whole trip in one shared place. Everyone sees the same restaurants, attractions, neighborhoods, notes, maps, and itinerary. It runs as a hosted web app with a free database behind it, and for the handful of people I travel with, it costs essentially nothing.
 
I built it for Paris. Then I went to Paris and barely used it, which in retrospect feels about right.
 
Paris became the first essay in this series, [A Builder in Paris: Do Devs Dream of Électrique Chats?](https://dev.to/earlgreyhot1701d/a-builder-in-paris-do-devs-dream-of-electrique-chats-3hd9) I had deliberately put the computer down, and I found out that stepping away from the keyboard did not mean stepping away from building. Ideas have an annoying habit of following you.
 
New Orleans gave me the opposite experience. This time I put the computer down, and something I had already built followed me.
 
## An old app gets on a plane
 
Calling Le Voyage old feels strange, but the first real feature work started on December 28, 2025. By the time we landed in New Orleans it had been around for about nine months, which is plenty of time for a vibecoded project to pile up features, assumptions, forgotten decisions, and small mysteries left behind by an earlier version of yourself.
 
The GitHub repository has well over a hundred commits now. The README still more or less says "Welcome to your Lovable project," a leftover from the AI app builder I used to make it. Priorities. I was not trying to turn Le Voyage into a product. I was trying to catch a plane.
 
About a week before the trip, though, I started looking at the app differently, because this time I knew we were going to use it. That changes things. A filter that resets after a reload is mildly annoying at your desk. It is a lot more irritating when you are walking through an unfamiliar neighborhood trying to decide where to get breakfast.
 
So the app learned to remember our filter and map preferences for each trip. It got sorting, so sixty-eight places did not have to live in one giant pile. It got a confirmation step before deleting a place, because entries now had notes and itinerary links attached, and deleting one by accident had stopped being funny. The map interactions got better, categories became editable, and the AI feature got its usual maintenance when its model aged out.
 
None of those changes were glamorous. All of them mattered more than another shiny AI button would have. That may be the first thing New Orleans taught me about my own app: the boring parts of software become very important once you use it.
 
## Sixty-eight places and still hungry
 
Our first meal was at MRB in the French Quarter, which was already in Le Voyage. This is where one of the simplest features in the app earned its keep: the notes field.
 
My sister's notes were not polished travel writing. They looked like this:
 
> FQ, dive bar, "potent drinks," outdoor seating, "oyster bar"
 
Useful shorthand, enough to jog a memory. From the place card we could jump out to Google, read reviews, check the menu and the location, and decide whether it still sounded good now that we were standing there instead of researching it from home. It did. Excellent food. Everything fried. Oh yeah!
 
Somewhere around that first meal, Le Voyage stopped feeling like a project I had built and started feeling like an app I had. That distinction has been sitting with me. Most side projects stay verbs. You build them, deploy them, post a screenshot, maybe write an article, and then they sit quietly on a server while you chase the next idea.
 
A few become nouns. They live on your phone. You open them again. Someone besides you adds something, and then they add more than you do. They gain history.
 
My sister added most of the New Orleans places. Her notes were in there, her choices were in there, and we both opened the app first thing in the morning looking for breakfast and again while we wandered during the day. The trip wasn't my dataset. It was ours.
 
That made the weaknesses much easier to see. Le Voyage had solved the problem I originally designed it for, which was remembering all the places we were interested in. Unfortunately, we had been very successful. Now we had sixty-eight places to search through.
 
Breakfast? Scroll. Drinks? Scroll. Somewhere close? Scroll. Something quick because we had already walked enough for one day? Scroll some more.
 
The problem was no longer discovery. It was choosing. I don't think I could have learned that staring at the app on my laptop. At home, sixty-eight saved places looked like a feature. On Bourbon Street, they looked like work.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/6dymmxhgxj01crd3etbq.png)
 
## The AI feature finally found a job
 
Le Voyage already has an AI recommendation feature. Right now it mostly exists because the app was built during an era when every button apparently needed to consult a model. It works, it costs almost nothing, and it is not especially useful.
 
New Orleans showed me what its job should be. I do not need a model to tell me New Orleans has restaurants. Yelp has that covered. I also do not need it to search the whole city and hand me another list. We already had sixty-eight.
 
What would have helped is being able to say: we're in the French Quarter, we want breakfast, we want to walk, give us three places from our list. Or: we just want a drink. Or a snack. Or something highly rated nearby. Use our notes, use our categories, use the places we already decided we cared about, and help us narrow it down.
 
That changes the role of the AI completely. Instead of discovering the world for us, it helps us decide inside a world we already curated. That is a much more interesting feature to me now. It is also one I am trying very hard not to build before Oaxaca. More on that later.
 
## Then New Orleans ignored our database
 
Some of the best places we went were not among the sixty-eight. People recommended them to us.
 
We ended up at Deanie's in Bucktown because a local told us to go. Excellent choice. Someone else sent us to Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop back in the French Quarter. Also an excellent choice. Purple drank. Iykyk.
 
This is where New Orleans did something no amount of pre-trip research could. The app knew what we had researched. New Orleans knew what we hadn't.
 
That sounds obvious, but it changed how I think about what Le Voyage should become. When you design a travel app from your desk, you design around planning. You collect places, organize them, build an itinerary, add filters and ratings and neighborhoods, and convince yourself that with enough structure you can make the trip legible before you arrive.
 
Then you travel. Someone behind a bar tells you where to eat. Someone takes the time to explain which place is worth the walk. You change plans because you're tired, or because you smell something good, or because the place you thought was nearby is not nearby in any meaningful sense after eight hours on your feet. Travel keeps reminding you that it does not belong entirely to your itinerary.
 
That wasn't a failure of Le Voyage. It was something the app had not learned to make room for yet. Maybe there should be a lightweight way to tell the places we researched apart from the places the trip gave us. A "Local Tip" tag, or "Found Here." Something simple. I don't know yet.
 
What I do know is that the best recommendation engine we used in New Orleans was New Orleans. What I remember most clearly is not Bourbon Street, or even the Mississippi and the steamboats we walked past. It is the people. They had time. They said hello. They were friendly, charming, and knowledgeable, and they were happy to tell you where to go and then explain why.
 
There is something wonderfully humbling about spending months tinkering with travel software only to find out that one of its most valuable future features might be a better way to remember what somebody told you in a five-minute conversation.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/9d4z783l8mnhqfdknj0r.png)
 
## Maybe useful slop is still useful
 
There is another part of this I have been thinking about since we got home. Le Voyage is vibecoded. Very vibecoded. There is essentially no automated test suite.
 
So I'm not waving a flag for AI-generated software here. If Le Voyage moved money, ran infrastructure, handled medical information, or kept somebody's company running, I would be having a very different conversation with myself.
 
It doesn't. It is a travel app for me, my sister, my wife, and whichever friends come along on future trips. Free hosting, free database, and almost no running cost beyond the occasional AI call, which, as I already admitted, barely earns its keep.
 
And yet it gave us something useful: the same information, at the same time. My sister did not have one list while I had another, my wife had screenshots, somebody else had a Yelp collection, and the rest of the names disappeared into a group chat. We had one shared trip, one shared set of notes, one place where the stuff we cared about lived. That is different from opening another "Top 10 New Orleans Restaurants" list written for everybody. Commercial travel software has scale. Our little app has context.
 
That makes me wonder whether there is a category of software vibecoding is unusually well suited for: software for six people. Not six million. Six. Maybe even two. Software so specific nobody would build a company around it, but cheap enough now that one person can make it anyway.
 
Whenever a side project turns out to be useful, I notice the same question showing up in my head: what happens next? Do you monetize it? Add Stripe? Get users? Build onboarding? Turn the pleasant little thing into a SaaS and eventually spend a Saturday staring at a retention dashboard?
 
I don't think I want to. Will I keep Le Voyage alive? Yes, for now. Will I monetize it? Probably not. I like that it can be weirdly specific to us. I like that "FQ" is enough explanation. I like that my sister's notes do not need to make sense to an addressable market.
 
I don't think software has to become a business to justify existing. Sometimes you make a thing, two people use it, then maybe four, and it makes their trip a little easier. For me, that can be enough.
 
## The app matured before the idea did
 
That may be the part I find most interesting now. Over nine months, Le Voyage itself grew up. It learned to remember things, got better maps, made deletion safer, and improved its sorting. The rough edges got filed down one at a time.
 
But I don't think I understood the product as well as I thought I did. I thought the problem was collecting places for a trip. New Orleans taught me that collecting was the easy part. The harder problem was deciding what to do with all those places once the trip started moving around us.
 
That is a different product, and I only found it because we used the thing. Not tested it. Used it. There is a difference there too. Testing asks whether the software behaves the way you expect. Using it has a nasty habit of asking whether your expectations made sense in the first place.
 
## Oaxaca is next
 
At the end of this month, Le Voyage is coming with me to Oaxaca. Naturally, I now have ideas, and this is the dangerous part.
 
I want the contextual recommendation feature. I want a better way to capture the places locals tell us about. I want better search. I want the app to understand that "nearby" means something very different at 9 a.m. than it does after dinner when everyone's feet hurt.
 
Because this is a vibecoded app, I could probably open Lovable and start changing half of it tonight. That is exactly why I am trying not to. There are real trips in that database now, and real notes. My sister uses it. I use it. And my current automated test coverage is approximately "open the app and start clicking."
 
My younger vibecoder instinct says there is plenty of time before Oaxaca to add something cool. The part of me that has spent more time around software since I first built Le Voyage says I should find out what I am about to break before I add anything. So QA first. Probably.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/bcusgzddyod922wgs1t2.png)
 
In Paris, I learned that stepping away from the computer did not mean stepping away from building, sometimes especially when the laptop was shut. New Orleans taught me something slightly different. Sometimes you have to stop building long enough to find out whether the thing you built belongs in your life.
 
Le Voyage does. It is unfinished. The AI feature needs a real job. The README is embarrassing. The tests are, at the moment, more of a philosophical position than a software artifact.
 
But my sister and I used it. Then we used it again. And now it has a ticket to Oaxaca.
 
For now, that's enough.
 
AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

The “software for six people, not six million” part really clicked for me. There’s a technical consequence to that which is easy to miss: once the app is built around a small, trusted dataset, the AI doesn’t need to be the source of truth anymore. It can become a decision layer on top of the user’s actual context.

For example, instead of asking an LLM, “What are the best breakfast places in the French Quarter?”, the app could first narrow the user’s own records:

places
 .where(category: "breakfast")
 .where(neighborhood: "French Quarter")
 .where("walking_minutes <= ?", 15)
 .order(rating: :desc)
 .limit(3)

 Enter fullscreen mode
 

 Exit fullscreen mode
 

Then the model only has to explain or rank those three based on notes, preferences, and the current situation.

That distinction matters a lot with AI features. Retrieval/filtering gives you the boundary; the model handles the messy human part. Otherwise you end up building another Yelp with a chatbot attached.

And your “test vs use” point is probably the bigger lesson here. A filter resetting on reload is easy to call a minor bug until you're standing on Bourbon Street trying to use the thing. Real usage has a funny way of turning “edge cases” into requirements.

title: Crowdwide is ALMOST DONE!! WOOOHOOO!! 🎉🚀
author: Puneet-Kumar2010
body:
So… after weeks of building, fixing, breaking, fixing again, questioning my life choices, and repeating the same cycle…

**Crowdwide is almost done!!** 😭🎉

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/d59eelc3uosv6grhdz6r.webp)
And by almost done, I mean almost ready for its first stable release!

GitHub: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide
Live website: https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

I dont wanted crowdwide to just look like a simple social network platform so at first I thought that i will build all the features like common social media platform have and then i will add some my own feature ... 

When I first started building Crowdwide, I thought about all the features a social media platform should have.

Chat? Done.
Group chats? Done.
Sharing links? Done.
Media uploads? Done.
Communities? Done.
Posts, articles, polls, reactions, bookmarks, notifications… all those usual social media features? Done!

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/4cc7padff7xrobhf8es1.png)


But then I started thinking…

*If other platforms already have these features, what can I build that makes Crowdwide feel a little different?*

I didn't want to build just another social media platform with the same features arranged in a slightly different UI.

So I started looking for ideas, exploring other platforms, and thinking about what else communities and their members could do.

And I found some pretty NOICE ideas!! 😂

## 🗺️ 1. Community Map — THIS IS SO COOL!!

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/r886qhn9cmr49beplx9m.png)


Imagine opening a map and seeing communities from different places represented on it.

That's the idea!

Community owners can choose to show their community on the map. And here's the fun part: **the bigger the community, the bigger its dot on the map!**

So, as a community grows, its presence on the map grows too.

Just imagine zooming out and seeing communities popping up across different places. It makes the platform feel a little more alive, doesn't it?

And honestly, when I started building this, I kept thinking:

*BROOO, THIS LOOKS SO COOL!!* 😭
AND THIS ONE IS MY FAVORITE FEATURE IN CROWDWIDE MY OWN SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFROM
UK ONE THING THAT I LIKE IS IN MY OWN CREATIONS IS IF I NEED ANYTHING I CAN JUST ADD IT... THIS IS THE EXAMPLE OF THAT 

Of course, building it was a whole different story. More on that later…

## 🏆 2. Community Quests and Challenges

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/yoa6526envzujivz8v6i.png)
as you can see I won the quest created by me thats smart move 🙄🦊

I came across a quest-like challenge on DEV and thought…

*Wait a minute. Why not bring something like this to Crowdwide communities?*

So I added the concept of **community quests**!

A community can create a quest or challenge, announce it to its members, and declare a winner.

And the winner? They get a badge on their profile! 🏅

I want communities to be places where people don't just scroll through posts but also participate in things together.

There are still some limitations, though. My budget is… well… let's not talk about it. 😂

I'm 15, still under 18, and working with free resources, so some things are harder to set up than others.
I Really wanted to building something like that give some real rewards
But the feature is part of the plan, and I hope to keep improving it!

## 🎧 3. Personal Recap — Inspired by Spotify

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/a9qt21rr8acaet4x4rzy.png)
I'm the most active user of this platform! The OG myself... lol

You know Spotify Wrapped and those personal recaps that show what you've been listening to, discovering, and enjoying?

That got me thinking.

What if Crowdwide could give users a recap of their activity on the platform?

Things like:

* What topics they were interested in.
* What new things they discovered.
* What they shared the most.
* A summary of their activity and interests.

So, I added a **Personal Recap** section!

For now, it's just the beginning. As Crowdwide collects more useful activity statistics, I can add more interesting insights to it.

Imagine looking back at your activity and discovering what your internet-self was up to. 👀

## ✍️ 4. Co-authors on Posts?!

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/tddl0apqx13sgv8rlsz4.png)


Here's another concept I wanted to try.

What if a post could have two authors instead of just one?

Not just tagging someone or mentioning them in the post. I mean actual **co-authorship**!

Both owners can edit the same post.

I think this could be useful for people collaborating on announcements, community updates, articles, or other shared content.

And yes, it's in Crowdwide now!

## 💬 5. Some More Features!

Apart from the new ideas, I also added some things that were missing from the platform.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ud9q9e1hj5be943xl1j0.png)
btw mansio is so busy that he never replies ... keep it up mansio

Things like:

* GIF support.
* Sending media in chats.
* Searching messages within chats.
* Group chat details and settings.
* More complete group chat functionality.

These might sound like small things, but they make the overall experience feel much more complete.

And that's the thing about building a platform: you keep finding little things that you somehow forgot to add earlier. 😂

## 🐛 Things I Learned the HARD Way

Now comes the fun part.

Actually, no.

The PAINFUL part. AAAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHH!! 😭

Building Crowdwide taught me a lot, but some lessons came with a ridiculous amount of frustration.

### 1. API keys can waste HOURS of your life

I've been keeping Crowdwide in development for over a month, testing features and fixing bugs.

Sometimes, an API key gets revoked, expires, or stops working as expected.

And what do I do?

I see an error, assume something is wrong with my code, and start debugging.

I check the logic.
I inspect the endpoint.
I rewrite things.
I question everything.

And then I discover that the actual problem was the API key.

BROOOOOOOOOOO.

ALL THAT TIME. ALL THAT CODE. FOR AN API KEY?! 😭

Lesson learned: **check your credentials and service status before spending hours debugging your code.**

Please learn from my suffering.

### 2. Adding a map is NOT as easy as it looks

I thought adding a map would be straightforward.

Just get the map, plot the communities, adjust the markers, and done!

HAHAHAHAHAHA. NO.

I ran into API restrictions, policies, unavailable endpoints, configuration problems, and errors that seemed to appear out of nowhere.

One moment, something worked. The next moment, another endpoint refused to cooperate.

I spent so much time figuring out what was wrong.

But eventually, I got it working!

And seeing the result made the struggle feel worth it. 🗺️

### 3. TRANSLATIONS. WHY ARE YOU LIKE THIS?!

Okay, this one is still haunting me.

The translation functionality works on my local device, but it's not working properly in the deployed version.

And I've been trying to figure out why.

Same project. Same feature. Different environment. Different problems.

AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHH.

I'm still working on this, and I hope to get it fixed in a future update.

For now, the rest of the platform is working, but translations may not work as expected for everyone.

I'll keep working on it!

### 4. Being broke while building a platform 💀

Another challenge: I don't have a credit card.

So I'm relying heavily on free tiers, free services, and whatever resources I can find.

And finding free services that actually fit your requirements, setting them up, understanding their limitations, and making everything work together?

Sometimes it feels like chewing nuts through your nose.

WHY IS IT SO HARD?! 😭

But honestly, working with these limitations has also taught me to be more resourceful.

You learn to research, experiment, find alternatives, and work with what you have.

Still, if I ever get the chance to move Crowdwide to proper paid infrastructure, I WILL CELEBRATE.

## 💰 Community Monetization Is Still Coming!

One of the bigger features I want to introduce is community monetization.

The idea is to let community owners monetize their communities, somewhat like how creators can monetize content on platforms such as Blogger.

I want community owners to have more opportunities to grow their communities and potentially earn from them.

However, setting this up properly requires more work, research, and resources.

So, monetization isn't ready yet.

The same goes for some of the more advanced possibilities around quests and community features. I'll keep working on these as Crowdwide grows.

## 🧠 What Building Crowdwide Taught Me

This project has taught me much more than just how to write code.

I've learned about:

* Building and maintaining a large application.
* Integrating third-party APIs.
* Debugging production-only issues.
* Handling authentication and account security.
* Designing features around communities.
* Working with limited resources.
* Understanding that a feature working locally doesn't mean it'll work in production.
* And, most importantly, that building a project is one thing, but making it reliable is a whole different journey.

I've also learned that sometimes the best ideas come when you're trying to solve a completely different problem.

And sometimes, you spend three hours debugging something that turns out to be a revoked API key.

Both experiences are equally educational, I guess. 💀

## 🚀 TOMORROW IS THE DAY!

Okay, enough talking.

**Crowdwide's first stable release is almost here!**

Tomorrow, October 3, 2026, I'll clear the test data and prepare the platform for its first stable version: **Crowdwide v1**.

So, if you want to check it out, create an account, explore the communities, and try things out, you can do so today.

Just remember that **all test data will be cleared on October 3, 2026**. Anything you create before the reset may be deleted.

After the reset, the platform will be ready to start fresh!

### 🔗 Check it out!

🌐 **Live website:** https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

💻 **GitHub repository:** https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

And yes, it's OPEN SOURCE!!

Also, the repository currently has **0 stars**.

FAAAAAAAAHHHHHHH. 😭

It's okay, though. If nobody stars it, I'll just star my own repository.

PROBLEM SOLVED. 😂⭐

## ❤️ A Small Request

Right now, Crowdwide is running entirely on free-tier resources.

That means there may occasionally be unexpected issues, limitations, or downtime. If you encounter a bug, please let me know!

And if you'd like to contribute, you're welcome to explore the repository, create a branch, make improvements, and submit a pull request.

I'd genuinely appreciate the help.

I'm hoping that, over the next 6–8 months or so, as Crowdwide grows and I find the resources to support it, I can move it to better infrastructure, get a proper domain, and use more reliable database and hosting solutions.

For now, we're making the most of what we have!

## One Last Thing…

Crowdwide isn't perfect yet.

Translations still need work, monetization isn't ready.
For now all the main core features are done just tranlation is broken (working on my device but on deployed it brokes!?? dirty translator!!)

But seeing something that started as an idea slowly turn into a working platform is an amazing feeling.

I'm just 15, and this is one of the biggest projects I've worked on so far. Before this i tried to build one social media platform but that was not very good like u can post and after some time you'd find that your post's banner was missing ... yea that was supremacy of my old platform vibeconnet (its deleted 2 min silence for it... lol)

There were bugs, frustrating days, broken APIs, confusing documentation, and moments when I genuinely wondered why I was doing all this.

But here we are.

**Crowdwide is almost ready for its first stable release!**

And this is just version 1. There's still so much more I want to do.

Thank you to everyone who checks it out, reports bugs, contributes, or simply takes a look.

Now excuse me while I prepare for the release and hope nothing breaks tomorrow.

PLEASE. NOTHING. BREAK. TOMORROW. 😭🙏

**WOOOHOOOOOO!! 🎉🚀**

title: Why you still need a Website Portfolio, even though everyone can Vibe Code it.
author: FrancisTRᴅᴇᴠ
body:
If you have been following me for a long time, you already know that I have been holding off on my Portfolio review for several months. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/55r34irqjs415ihk0o1e.gif)   **Before you ask, yes, I will finally show my portfolio website.** First, I want to write about something we all may have been thinking about at some point.   **Everyone needs a developer portfolio.** It's one of the big ways to stand out in the tech market because it shows your work and experience to recruiters in a friendly UI format. Some may say it's a great alternative to review a candidate's work **(Source: Trust me bro).** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7h8pveibft5pc28guc01.png) However, in the age of AI, it seems that it's almost impossible to create a portfolio that stands out. **Why is that the case?**   ## AI Can do...anything? We all (probably) have tried using AI at some point and even still use AI in our daily lives. Whether how much you have used it, you probably already know its capabilities. **AI is trained so well that it can potentially one-shot a website portfolio.** Even better, if the person decides, it can add features and other stuff to make the website look like it was built in months (even though it was built in minutes). We even got to the point where **Claude was able to merge two games into one in a matter of a few weeks!** {% embed https://www.youtube.com/shorts/xo3vpvbA8p8 %} **It's crazy isn't it.** AI development has been rapidly growing in the last few years to the point where it is accomplishing tasks that may have taken months to do. With that said, I thought to myself: **"Why consider building a portfolio if everyone can vibe code their way into making their perfect portfolio?"** To be honest, it's a valid question. The market has been difficult because **everyone is using AI to their advantage to stand out from the market.** I have seen a lot of Website Portfolios and Resumes that have been assisted with AI. **As a result, the bar has never been higher.** However, I still believe having a portfolio still matters, even in this age where it seems impossible. **Here's my reasoning.**   ---   ## AI Portfolios may look different, but they are the same. **What do I mean by this?** I am talking about **"style".** If you try to vibe code a portfolio, people can tell that the portfolio is vibe coded. Sure, it's not the EXACT replica compare to 100 portfolios out there, but you can easily tell by seeing some UI features that are defaulted if you vaguely prompt it. A small example is this: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/1floz2r2trb7qglvp6l7.png) I have reviewed a lot of portfolios that has this (or something similar). Sure this may be a coincidence, but I want you to try to vibe code a sample website portfolio. Most of the time, they will add this feature. This matters because if you think about it, a lot of portfolios out there are simply the same, **even though it may not look like it.** You have to have good "attention to detail" to see this for sure. However, at this point, coming from a person who has reviewed candidates before, it tends to be **really repetitive.** Hence, making it harder in the hiring process since everyone is doing the same thing and more research needs to be accounted for. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/otitvym1xxhlr917bsuf.png) This leads to the next point.   ## "New Mask, Same Task" ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/iyhst5tknfvs08r0i8wn.png) **Yes, I took this straight up from RDJ.** Though the whole point is that even though he plays a different character, **he is still RDJ.** **What does this mean in this context?** Just because you have pretty portfolio, **it does not mean your work reflects that.** You can create many different portfolios under your name. At the end of the day, **it's still you that needs to improve and not the portfolio.** **Portfolio is used as a presentation.** If you are presenting your portfolio and it looks good, I would assume you have a lot of work experience and projects that are noticeable based on your portfolio design and how you are selling yourself. For example, you have a front-end developer portfolio, **but if I were to investigate further into your GitHub, I may see the following things:** - You just joined as of this year on GitHub. - You claimed you did Open-Source, but there is no PR that reflects that. - Your Portfolio has good UI, your project doesn't. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hqqedl0o60hmgy3vmbwq.png) I can list a lot of things, but the main point is that if you have a good portfolio with a good list of projects you have done, **you better hope that your projects and work reflects on how you built this portfolio.** This is **ESPECIALLY** true if you tried to become a front-end developer. If your UI is good, you better hope your projects reflects that. It's something to keep in mind when building your portfolio. Of course, if you are applying for a back-end developer role, having a good UI on your website portfolio isn't really required, but it's a nice to have. **The whole point is to not misrepresent yourself. Be careful on what you add on your portfolio. Always assume people will have questions on your work.**     Those are the two main things. Though you may be asking **"How do I make my portfolio stand out"?** **Here are some key things that you can do (and yes, I am now showing my portfolio lol).**   ---   ## 1. Start with a basic portfolio template, then use AI to add onto it. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/nl747eyej271ayfn2iit.png) For my case, I have used an existing portfolio from **"brittanychiang.com and meikopoulos.com"**. From there, I grab existing features using AI and put them together into a portfolio I am proud of. Additionally, I added some new features that are not distracting, but is something I want to add onto my portfolio to make it unique to me: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/y6mihaafktq4gfkff5ut.png) **Instead of building it from scratch, I encourage you to find a portfolio that already exists (Bonus points: Proven that it stands out in the tech market) and build it on top of it.** This allows the portfolio to be unique and that **reflects you.** Additionally, building on to of a template is a good starting point because it already has the fundamentals on what makes a portfolio "good". In this case, I added a feature where the "Skills" section reveals Pokemon in each Skill Card, though I am not sharing how it works. **Can you find the Easter egg that does that?** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vvvd3q57f49bbfmctdxz.png)   ## 2. Usability and Accessibility! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/kqbmxzxpo3fhlxop36kf.png) **This is the most OVERLOOK aspect of making a portfolio.** Even though you can make your portfolio look nice, it's most likely that it's **not accessible.** **For example, it can be very laggy on low-end devices, not responsive on mobile, not following best practices, etc.** There are a lot of things that is overlooked because we focus on building the best looking portfolio where we should be focusing on making our website portfolio optimized. I would recommend spending time using AI to optimize your portfolio. In other words: **"Boil the lake to make the portfolio, but boil the ocean for website optimization and accessibility".** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/shabozho5fs63ftadpah.png) **For mine, I spend countless prompts where I tell the AI to make sure my portfolio is less "laggy" and being able to run on mobile.** This will allow to make a much cleaner portfolio and being able to be used by many people such as people who have disabilities, devices that are not powerful, etc.   ## 3. Simplicity beats Complexity! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3jdxudp8a03vvlni8jvj.png) **A lot of portfolios we have seen tends to be very complex where there are a lot of animations and such.** However, the more you think about it, the more you realized that you can **stand out easily.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8pa5pdohs07xc78ycnsv.png) I have seen a lot of portfolios that are REALLY complex and have a lot of animations, but what people fail to realized is that: **You are doing what everyone else is doing.** **At the end of the day, you are not standing out, even if you THINK that you are.** If I see a portfolio that is heavily designed using AI, I can guarantee that I can find the exact same person who can one-up that. **The best advice is making it simple.** Yes, it's boring and yes it's common. But..that's the whole point. I rarely see any portfolio that is simply built. **Usually the ones that are simple tends to stand out because it shows a lot of information really quickly.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/yprh442j56lfeei9e71u.png) **This is huge because recruiters tends to review portfolios and resumes in seconds.** They will not have time to look over your awesome UI and animation you have Vibe Coded. The UI should be the icing on the cake, not the whole cake. **The most important parts is your work and experience.** Then why design your portfolio? You don't need a portfolio. That simply isn't true - a total myth. They're generally just curated vanity projects that tell a potential employer next to nothing about the reality of a candidate's abilities. Vibe coding giúp dựng UI nhanh, nhưng portfolio không chỉ là "có trang web" — nó là bằng chứng tư duy.

Portfolio vẫn là "source of truth" duy nhất mà bạn kiểm soát trọn vẹn — không phụ thuộc algorithm LinkedIn, không bị GitHub ẩn repo khi đổi policy, và quan trọng nhất: nó ép bạn phải curate thay vì chỉ dump code.

Thấy nhiều dev junior bỏ qua phần "why" trong project: tại sao chọn stack này? Trade-off gì? Bug gì khổ nhất và fix như thế nào? AI viết được code, nhưng chưa thể fake được battle scars và decision-making process. Đó mới là món hàng nhà tuyển dụng thực sự mua.

As a mobile developer (not really frontend), I completely agree with starting from a good example instead of from scratch. And "the UI should be the icing, not the whole cake" is the line I'll remember.

One honest UX moment: I tried to click your bouncing circles. I assumed each one was a project, with its main technology written on it, and that it would take me to the repo 😄 It made me realize what I look for in a portfolio: meaning first, beauty second.

That matters to me now because I don't want to be "only" a mobile developer anymore. I want to think about UX, watch the funnel myself, learn security: all the things I never had time for. So for me, a portfolio should show reasoning (why I chose this, what I rejected, what I learned), not just finished, pretty projects.

You will be surprised on how many people fail this part because they tend to focus more about making the website run and look nice instead of explaining why it was built this way.

comments.text:
The observation that vibe-coded portfolios look different on the surface and still feel the same underneath matches what hiring managers keep saying quietly. Layout variety went up. Evidence of judgment did not.

What still separates a useful portfolio is not how fast the homepage appeared. It is whether the visitor can see a decision that cost something: a trade-off you made, a constraint you accepted, a feature you refused, or a production incident you owned. AI can invent screens. It is much worse at inventing a credible trail of choices.

One practical habit that helps: for each project, write three lines that a model would not invent for you. Who the user was, what almost failed in production, and what you would not do the same way. That is usually enough for a recruiter to tell whether the site is a render or a record of work.

comments.author: Paolo Ronco
comments.text:
I agree with your point about simplicity. A portfolio should show what someone has actually built, not just how good they are at generating a nice-looking interface with AI.

I'm a cybersecurity analyst, and I maintain my own website at paoloronco.it, where I share my projects, technical articles, and things I've learned along the way.

One of those projects is OrbitPage, an open-source page builder I've been developing. It started as a personal project and gradually evolved into a platform with a hosted SaaS version and a self-hosted, MIT-licensed core.

I think the open-source aspect is particularly important here. Having the source code publicly available on GitHub means people can look beyond screenshots and descriptions to see how a project is actually built, maintained, and improved over time. The architecture, commit history, documentation, security fixes, and technical decisions can say a lot more about someone's skills than a polished landing page.

Building OrbitPage has also pushed me to learn a lot about full-stack development, cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, DevOps, and product design, which are things I wouldn't necessarily be able to demonstrate through a traditional resume.

That's where I think personal portfolios still have real value. The website is just the presentation layer. What matters is the actual work, experience, and learning behind it.

Since you're reviewing portfolios, I'd be curious to hear what you think of mine, especially from a usability and presentation perspective.

Regardless of that, it looks like your portfolio is stacked, which is good for your case if you have more experience. Those who just started, I would recommend the opposite (not adding too much). For this case, it's normal.

The one thing I would recommend not to add is measuring your skills. Even though it's good to be honest with yourself, it's also a double edge-sword. If you are applying for a role that needs an expertise in Cryptography, then you shot yourself in the foot. Additionally, you may think you know that much of that skill, but you will never know until they test you. I would remove measuring your skills. comments.author: Paolo Ronco
comments.text:
Hey Francis! Thanks a lot for taking the time to review my portfolio and for the kind words about OrbitPage! Really appreciate it.

You make a very good point about measuring skills. It's actually something I've thought about quite a bit while building my website. I eventually decided to include skill levels because I felt they could give visitors a quick overview of where I stand across different technologies. But I definitely see the downside: self-assessments are subjective, and what I consider a certain level of expertise might not match someone else's expectations, especially during an interview.

I'll give this some more thought and perhaps revisit that section in the future, maybe with a little help from AI as well!

Regarding simplicity, I also think there's an interesting distinction between someone with years of experience and someone just starting out. When you're at the beginning of your journey, you might not have many projects, certifications, or professional experiences to showcase yet. But I don't think that should stop anyone from having their own little corner of the internet.

That's actually one of the ideas behind OrbitPage. Not everyone needs to build a full portfolio from scratch or spend hours designing one. Sometimes a simple, ready-to-use page with your name, a short introduction, contact information, and a few links is already a great starting point. You can then expand it naturally as you learn, build projects, and gain experience.

And that brings us back to the original discussion: AI and modern tools have made creating a website easier than ever, but the real value still comes from the person and the content behind it.

Thanks again for the thoughtful feedback and for checking out my work!

What helps is treating the AI output as a first draft and then making the deliberate choices yourself: one typeface pairing you actually like, a consistent spacing scale, a single accent color, and at least one detail that's clearly yours (your Pokémon easter egg is a good example). Those small decisions are what visitors remember, and they're usually quicker to make by adjusting the page directly than by re-prompting. Disclosure: We work on Tado Studio, an Astro site builder where AI makes the first version and you then click elements to adjust them with the code alongside. It's coming soon: https://tadostudio.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=prelaunch&ref=1012-devto-portfolio#join
